recall.a: Actors + use-case ovals + associations showing who participates in what. Include = factored-out shared sub-flow (dashed, arrow to included). Generalisation = actor B can do everything A can plus more. Never a sequence of steps.
recall.q: What belongs on a use-case diagram, and what do include/generalisation mean?

sections.heading: Introduction
paras: A UML use-case diagram shows the names of all use cases, all actors, and which actors participate in which use cases — a map of scope, not a story. The lecture is unusually frank: use-case diagrams have limited usefulness next to written descriptions. They show who is involved in what; the description carries the actual requirements.

sections.heading: The vocabulary
paras: Ovals are use cases at task level (Watch Video, Upload Video, Report Video in the running video-sharing example). Stick figures are actors; lines (associations) show participation — the 'who does what' view. The include relationship factors out a shared sub-flow used by several cases (dashed arrow toward the included case): one 'Authenticate User' included by many cases beats five copies. Actor generalisation means one actor can do everything another can, plus more (a moderator does all a viewer does, plus moderation).

The lecture's warning slide — 'Use Case Diagrams Are Not Flow Charts!' — shows a fake diagram chaining steps (Uploader → Pick Video → ...) and rejects it: sequencing belongs in the written flow, never in arrows between ovals.

sections.heading: Scope and goal level
paras: The closing slides add design scope (which system are we even describing?) and goal level (summary vs user-goal vs sub-function). Most exam diagrams want user-goal ovals for the system under consideration — if you draw login-administration-summary cases alongside real goals, you signal you cannot tell levels apart.

summary: Use-case diagrams map actors to goal-ovals with include and generalisation — scope overviews whose detail lives in the written descriptions, never flowcharts.
